… or some practice them by strenuous effort; but when they reach achievement, it is one and the same. The Master said: "To be fond of learning is near to wisdom; to practice with vigor is near to benevolence; to possess the feeling of shame is near to courage."

Mo Weize 莫維則

Associate Examiner Instructor Zou 鄒 comments: In the topic, "one and the same" (yi 一) and "near" (jin 近) directly correspond to each other. This composition grasps the crucial point best, and its diction is moreover poised and refined. Record it for publication.
Examiner Instructor Hu 胡 comments: Precise in principle and orderly in diction.
Examiner Instructor Chen 陳 comments: A piece of great elegance.

In discussing people with respect to the universal virtues, in their ultimate sum they are one and the same, and in seeking them they are near at hand. Indeed, to be one and the same in the end is the completion of virtue; to be near at the beginning is the entry into virtue. How could those who learn through painful effort or practice by strenuous effort excuse themselves? Moreover, as for the universal virtues in humanity, their principle is fundamentally one and not two, and their motivating mechanism is fundamentally near and not far; it simply depends on how much effort a person makes for himself.

When the Way is manifested in a person, one need not be born with knowledge before one can speak of knowing it. Whether one attains it through learning or attains it through painful effort, although each seems to have its own manner of knowing, when we observe them after they have come to know, there are no two kinds of knowing. Why is this? Because the Way in essence stops simply at being able to know. When the Way is embodied in a person, one need not practice it with natural ease before one can speak of practicing it. Whether it comes through advantage or comes through strenuous effort, although each seems to have its own manner of practice, when we observe them after they have reached achievement, there are no two kinds of practice. Why is this? Because the Way in essence stops simply at being able to practice.

Now, in knowing one can observe wisdom, in practicing one can observe benevolence, and in the oneness of wisdom and benevolence one can observe courage. As for those who have not yet been able to become one, how are they to draw near to it? In the world…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
下不皆生知知未易幾也惟學而好焉勵一求
通之心則何蔽不可祛而知近矣天下不皆安
行仁未易幾也惟行而力焉持一邁往之心則
何私不可克而仁近矣天下不皆知盡仁至之
人勇未易幾也惟知恥焉存一愧悟之心則何
懦不可起知與成功之一而勇近矣是蓋道隨
人而可行二之卽非道德隨人而可入遠之卽
非德知所求焉卽由近而一何難哉雖然近之
易一之難也故虞庭之傳心曰一夫子之貫道
===
曰一是二者聖學也帝治也此夫子本之行道
之一推之九經之一正欲舉其君於堯舜文武
耳若曰卑之無甚高論豈識聖人告君之心哉
稷思天下有饑者由巳饑之也
吳正偉
同考試官訓導楊批聖人憂民饑處正在不
能人人敎稼穡上此作描寫精神入微矣
同考試官敎諭姜批格高詞偉鏗然乎希世
之音也可以式矣
punctuated:
下不皆生知，知未易幾也。惟學而好焉，勵一求通之心，則何蔽不可祛，而知近矣！天下不皆安行，仁未易幾也。惟行而力焉，持一邁往之心，則何私不可克，而仁近矣！天下不皆知盡仁至之人，勇未易幾也。惟知恥焉，存一愧悟之心，則何懦不可起？知與成功之一，而勇近矣！是蓋道隨人而可行，二之卽非道；德隨人而可入，遠之卽非德。知所求焉，卽由近而一，何難哉？雖然，近之易，一之難也。故虞庭之傳心曰「一」，夫子之貫道曰「一」。是二者，聖學也，帝治也。此夫子本之行道之一，推之九經之一，正欲舉其君於堯、舜、文、武耳。若曰「卑之無甚高論」，豈識聖人告君之心哉？

稷思天下有饑者，由巳饑之也。
吳正偉
同考試官訓導楊批：聖人憂民饑處，正在不能人人敎稼穡上。此作描寫精神入微矣。
同考試官敎諭姜批：格高詞偉，鏗然乎希世之音也，可以式矣。
translation_en:
…not everyone in the world is born with knowledge, so wisdom is not easily attained. Only by being fond of learning and rousing a mind determined to seek comprehension—what obscurity cannot be dispelled? Thus one comes close to wisdom! Not everyone in the world practices with effortless ease, so humanity is not easily attained. Only by practicing with strenuous effort and maintaining a mind that presses boldly forward—what selfishness cannot be overcome? Thus one comes close to humanity! Not everyone in the world is a person of exhaustive wisdom and utmost humanity, so courage is not easily attained. Only by possessing a sense of shame and preserving a mind of remorseful awakening—what cowardice cannot be roused to action? When attaining knowledge and achieving success become one, one comes close to courage! This is because the Way can be practiced according to the person—to treat it as dual is not the Way; virtue can be entered according to the person—to treat it as distant is not virtue. If one knows what to seek, then what difficulty is there in proceeding from coming close to achieving oneness? Even so, coming close to it is easy, whereas achieving oneness is difficult. Therefore, the transmission of the mind at the court of Yu (Shun) was called "oneness," and the Master's thread running through the Way was called "oneness." These two are the learning of the sages and the governance of the emperors. Here the Master rooted it in the oneness of practicing the Way and extended it to the oneness of the Nine Standard Rules, precisely wishing to elevate his ruler to the level of Yao, Shun, King Wen, and King Wu. If someone were to say, "Keep it modest and offer no overly lofty discourse," how could they understand the heart of the sage in counseling his ruler?

"Ji thought that if anyone in the world was starving, it was as if he himself had caused them to starve." [Mencius 4B.29]
By Wu Zhengwei 吳正偉.
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Yang comments: The point at which the sage worried about the people's starvation lay precisely in his inability to personally teach everyone sowing and reaping. This essay depicts that spirit with subtle penetration.
Associate Examiner and Instructor Jiang comments: Noble in structure and grand in diction, it rings with the resonant sound of a rare treasure in the world; it can serve as a model.

The sage minister thought anxiously of the hunger of his age, and took upon himself the responsibility for any failure to nourish them. Now, Hou Ji held the office of nourishing the people; if they lacked nourishment and went hungry, onto whom could the responsibility be shifted? Was this not why Hou Ji thought so deeply about it! Thus Mencius brought out the intention of Yu and Hou Ji in saving the people. Moreover, one who bears an office for all under Heaven ought to put the worries of all under Heaven first. Yu's office lay in controlling the waters, so he naturally thought that if anyone drowned it was caused by himself; what, then, did Hou Ji think? Indeed, Shun had worried about the people's hunger and entrusted the sowing of the hundred grains in their proper seasons to Hou Ji; Hou Ji had received Shun's command and took upon his own person the task of providing grain for the multitude of people. Since his office was named Director of Agriculture (Ji), he was truly the one upon whom all under Heaven relied for nourishment. And so in his heart, looking up and down, he pondered: "The Nine Provinces are so vast—how can my surveying and dividing of the land tread every single place? If there is even one place my surveying and dividing of the land has not reached, within the Nine Provinces might there not be someone empty-bellied and waiting to be fed? That someone is empty-bellied and waiting to be fed cannot be blamed on Heaven; it is simply on account of my office." As long as Hou Ji was in the world, he was truly the one upon whom all under Heaven depended to be free from hunger. And so in his heart, day and night, he pondered: "The common people are so numerous—how can I teach sowing and reaping to every single person? If my teaching of sowing and reaping is in any way incomplete, among the common people might there not be someone grieving and longing for a good harvest? That someone is grieving and longing for a good harvest cannot be blamed on other men; this is simply my own fault." He did not regard "by the sovereign's mandate feeding all without distinction" as a merit of assistance he had already achieved, but still regarded…

與彖傳曰人君以一人之身能使天下翕然從
punctuated:
庶奏艱食爲已未盡之責。惟其思之也深，故其救之也急，此稷之所以勤其官而爲天下烈與！大抵三代而上，君爲民立命；三代而下，民莫能自必其命。爲民立命者，視民饑由已；民莫必其命者，以爲饑於我何與焉。安有玉食萬方而恕然若是者？即能加意窮民，又或不罪已而罪歲。嗟乎！任人如舜，任事如稷，則阻饑之民，可轉而爲厚生之民。夫歲，固君人者自爲之也。

易

彖曰：「萃，聚也。順以說，剛中而應，故聚也。」
嚴旗先
同考試官教諭鄒批：發明上下萃道，詞不費，兩義自盡。
考試官教諭胡批：典確可誦。
考試官教諭陳批：精當。

《彖傳》釋《萃》之名義，以上下之一心也。夫情以一而聚也，卦之德、體，上下通爲一矣，此其所以萃與！《彖傳》曰：人君以一人之身，能使天下翕然從
translation_en:
… supplying the multitude with hard-won food as his own unfulfilled responsibility. Only because his concern was so deep was his relief so urgent. Is this not why Hou Ji was so diligent in his office and achieved such illustrious merit for the world? In general, during the Three Dynasties and earlier, the ruler established the destiny of the people; after the Three Dynasties, the people could no longer be assured of their own lives. Those who established the destiny of the people regarded the people's hunger as their own fault; under those beneath whom the people cannot be assured of their lives, the ruler thinks, "What has their hunger to do with me?" How can one enjoy the precious revenues of the myriad regions and yet remain so indifferent [恕然, read as 恝然]? Even if they manage to pay some heed to the destitute, they may still blame the harvest rather than themselves. Alas! If men are employed as Shun employed them, and affairs are undertaken as Hou Ji undertook them, then people suffering from famine can be transformed into people enjoying abundant livelihoods. Indeed, a good harvest is something that the ruler of men creates for himself.

Classic of Changes (Yi)

"The Commentary on the Decision (Tuan) says: 'Cui (Gathering Together) means congregating. Docile and yet joyous, firm in the center and finding response, therefore they congregate.'"
By Yan Qixian.
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Zou: It elucidates the Way of gathering together between above and below; without wasting words, both meanings [or: the meaning itself, taking 兩 as 而] are fully expressed.
Comment by Examiner Instructor Hu: Classical and precise, worthy of recitation.
Comment by Examiner Instructor Chen: Essential and fitting.

The Commentary on the Decision explains the name and meaning of the hexagram Cui (Gathering Together) in terms of the unity of mind between above and below. Feelings congregate when they are unified; in both the virtues and the structure of this hexagram, above and below are joined into one. Is this not why there is a gathering together? The Commentary on the Decision means to say: That a ruler of men, in his single person, is able to cause the whole world to harmoniously follow…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之而不忍離者無他焉有以一其心故也茲卦
之名曰萃則是天下有分土而無分民人心可
使聚而不可使散乃四海一家之時也於卦何
取哉蓋卦之德坤順兌說是順以從君者民也
而說道之使若實有以先之斯時也父母赤子
何其休戚之相關也卦之體剛中而應是誠實
下交者君也而虛中之誼臣又有以結之斯時
也元首股肱何其喜起之交協也上焉者聯屬
乎下則由朝廷而邦國而四方黎獻熈熈然其
===
若一人下焉者聯屬於上則由公卿而有司而
羣黎百姓藹藹然其若一心蓋方其未合也遠
而疎疎而渙即一堂之上已不相屬而况于民
及其旣合也羣而聚聚而親即萬里之遠可以
相通而况于近吾於是而知萃在天下而所以
使之萃者君也通于此而可以識萃之名義矣
雖然萃固難而保萃尤難夫人之一身四肢百
骸融而爲一苟精神元氣一日不貫即索然離
矣是故爲人君者運其精神以馭羣工培其元
punctuated: 之而不忍離者，無他焉，有以一其心故也。茲卦之名曰「萃」，則是天下有分土而無分民，人心可使聚而不可使散，乃四海一家之時也。於卦何取哉？蓋卦之德，坤順兌說，是順以從君者民也，而說道之使，若實有以先之。斯時也，父母赤子，何其休戚之相關也！卦之體，剛中而應，是誠實下交者君也，而虛中之誼，臣又有以結之。斯時也，元首股肱，何其喜起之交協也！上焉者聯屬乎下，則由朝廷而邦國、而四方黎獻，熈熈然其若一人；下焉者聯屬於上，則由公卿而有司、而羣黎百姓，藹藹然其若一心。蓋方其未合也，遠而疎，疎而渙，即一堂之上已不相屬，而况于民？及其旣合也，羣而聚，聚而親，即萬里之遠可以相通，而况于近？吾於是而知萃在天下，而所以使之萃者君也，通于此而可以識萃之名義矣。雖然，萃固難，而保萃尤難。夫人之一身，四肢百骸融而爲一，苟精神元氣一日不貫，即索然離矣。是故爲人君者，運其精神以馭羣工，培其元
translation_en: … him and cannot bear to part is for no other reason than that he has the means to unite their hearts. Now, that the name of this hexagram is "Gathering Together" (Cui) means that in the world there is division of territory, yet no division among the people; human hearts can be made to gather together and not be made to scatter—it is indeed a time when the Four Seas are a single family. From what in the hexagram is this meaning derived? Look at the virtues of the trigrams: Kun is docile and Dui is joyous. That which is docile in following the ruler is the people, while employing them by the way of joy seems truly to be what the ruler initiates first. At such a time, like parents and newborn babes, how closely bound are their joys and sorrows! Look at the structure of the hexagram: a firm line is central and finds response. That which interacts downward with sincere substance is the ruler, while with the bond of an open and receptive mind, the ministers in turn have the means to tie themselves to him. At such a time, like the head and the limbs, how harmonious is their mutual rejoicing and rising to action! When those above are joined to those below, then from the royal court to the feudal states and thedark-haired worthy ones of the four quarters, all are harmoniously thriving as though they were a single person; when those below are joined to those above, then from the dukes and ministers to the officials in charge and the multitude of common people, all are amiably united as though they were of a single mind. For before they have been brought together, distance leads to estrangement, and estrangement to dispersal—even within a single hall they are already disconnected from one another, how much more so with the common people! Yet once they have been brought together, they flock and gather, and gathering leads to affection—even across a distance of ten thousand li they can communicate with one another, how much more so with those nearby! From this I know that while gathering together takes place throughout the world, the one who causes them to gather together is the ruler; understanding this, one can recognize the meaning of the name "Gathering Together." Even so, to gather together is certainly difficult, and to preserve that gathering is harder still. In a person's body, the four limbs and hundred bones merge into one, yet if for a single day the vital spirit and primordial qi fail to circulate through them, they immediately fall apart in exhaustion. Therefore, for one who is a ruler of men, to exercise his vital spirit in governing all the officials and to cultivate the primordial…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
氣以厚黎民者保萃之道也
神也者妙萬物而爲言者也動萬物者莫
疾乎雷撓萬物者莫疾乎風燥萬物者
莫熯乎火說萬物者莫說乎澤潤萬物
者莫潤乎水終萬物始萬物者莫盛乎
艮故水火相逮雷風不相悖山澤通氣
然後能變化旣成萬物也
鄺行可
同考試官敎諭鄒批格高意渾而變化轉換
處絶無痕迹佳作也
考試官敎諭胡批是大家機軸錄之
考試官敎諭陳批思致筆力不凡
===
造物之妙神化相須者也夫一故神兩故化也
兩不可見而一神之用不幾於息哉大傳合先
後天而發之也若曰至矣造化之功其極天下
之至神者乎以爲倚於物也而未始滯於有以
爲離於物也而未始淪於無蓋妙萬物而爲言
者也何也天下之物成於造化而造物之功成
punctuated:
氣以厚黎民者，保萃之道也。

「神也者，妙萬物而爲言者也。動萬物者莫疾乎雷，撓萬物者莫疾乎風，燥萬物者莫熯乎火，說萬物者莫說乎澤，潤萬物者莫潤乎水，終萬物始萬物者莫盛乎艮。故水火相逮，雷風不相悖，山澤通氣，然後能變化，旣成萬物也。」

鄺行可
同考試官敎諭鄒批：格高意渾，而變化轉換處，絶無痕迹，佳作也。
考試官敎諭胡批：是大家機軸，錄之。
考試官敎諭陳批：思致筆力不凡。

造物之妙，神化相須者也。夫一故神，兩故化也。兩不可見，而一神之用，不幾於息哉？《大傳》合先後天而發之也。若曰：至矣造化之功，其極天下之至神者乎！以爲倚於物也，而未始滯於有；以爲離於物也，而未始淪於無。蓋妙萬物而爲言者也。何也？天下之物成於造化，而造物之功成
translation_en:
… primordial vitality so as to generously nurture the common people is the Way of preserving "gathering together" (Cui).

"Spirit (shen) is a term describing that which acts wondrously within the myriad things. For stirring the myriad things, nothing is swifter than thunder; for bending the myriad things, nothing is swifter than wind; for drying the myriad things, nothing is more parching than fire; for gladdening the myriad things, nothing is more gladdening than the marsh; for moistening the myriad things, nothing is more moistening than water; for bringing the myriad things to an end and giving the myriad things a beginning, nothing is more flourishing than keeping still (Gen). Therefore, water and fire complement each other, thunder and wind do not conflict with each other, and mountain and marsh communicate their vital breaths; only then can they transform and change, and bring all the myriad things to completion."

Kuang Xingke 鄺行可
Associate Examiner, Instructor Zou 鄒 comments: High in style and profound in meaning, and in the places where it transforms and transitions, it leaves no trace whatsoever—an excellent work.
Examiner, Instructor Hu 胡 comments: This has the structural mastery of a great writer; include it in the record.
Examiner, Instructor Chen 陳 comments: Its train of thought and vigor of brush are extraordinary.

In the wonder of creation, spirit and transformation depend upon one another. Now, because it is One, there is spirit; because it is Two, there is transformation. If the Two cannot be seen, would the functioning of the One spirit not nearly cease? The Great Treatise (Dazhuan) combines the Former Heaven (xiantian) and Later Heaven (houtian) sequences to expound upon this. It is as if to say: Supreme indeed is the achievement of creative transformation—does it not reach the utmost spirit in all under Heaven! If one takes it as relying upon things, it has never been mired in being; if one takes it as detached from things, it has never sunk into non-being. Indeed, it is a term describing that which acts wondrously within the myriad things. Why is this? The things of all under Heaven are brought to completion through creative transformation, and the achievement of creating things is brought to completion…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
於六子雷吾知其動物風吾知其撓物顧其所
以動且撓者雷風不與也神也火吾知其燥物
澤吾知其說物顧其所以燥且說者火澤不與
也神也水吾知其潤物艮吾知其終始物顧其
所以潤所以終始者坎艮不與也神也生成各
專其一而存主莫測其用所謂神妙萬物者非
耶然是六子之變化也豈自爲之運哉而物之
成也豈自爲之成哉吾觀於先天之卦水火則
相逮矣雷風則不相悖矣山澤則通氣矣而分
===
陰分陽者藏其宅夫是以變化之餘物得其潤
且燥焉物得其動且撓焉物得其說且成焉而
根陰根陽者神其功是變非他也陰之合於陽
而後變也化非他也陽之合於陰而後化也成
非他也陰陽之相須而成也故觀先天後天之
卦而神化合體用備矣大抵神統乎形神主其
逸而形任其勞者動靜之分也後天聖人退二
老于不用而生剋嗣續各因其時無非所以尊
神道耳噫造化之神常得於靜人心之神常失
punctuated: 於六子。雷，吾知其動物；風，吾知其撓物。顧其所以動且撓者，雷風不與也，神也。火，吾知其燥物；澤，吾知其說物。顧其所以燥且說者，火澤不與也，神也。水，吾知其潤物；艮，吾知其終始物。顧其所以潤、所以終始者，坎艮不與也，神也。生成各專其一，而存主莫測其用，所謂「神妙萬物」者，非耶？然是六子之變化也，豈自爲之運哉？而物之成也，豈自爲之成哉？吾觀於先天之卦，水火則相逮矣，雷風則不相悖矣，山澤則通氣矣，而分陰分陽者藏其宅。夫是以變化之餘，物得其潤且燥焉，物得其動且撓焉，物得其說且成焉，而根陰根陽者神其功。是變非他也，陰之合於陽而後變也；化非他也，陽之合於陰而後化也；成非他也，陰陽之相須而成也。故觀先天後天之卦，而神化合、體用備矣。大抵神統乎形，神主其逸而形任其勞者，動靜之分也。後天聖人退二老于不用，而生剋嗣續，各因其時，無非所以尊神道耳。噫！造化之神常得於靜，人心之神常失
translation_en: … through the six offspring-trigrams. As for thunder, I know that it stirs things into motion; as for wind, I know that it bends and scatters things. Yet as for that whereby they stir and bend things, thunder and wind have no part in it—it is spirit. As for fire, I know that it dries things; as for the marsh, I know that it gladdens things. Yet as for that whereby they dry and gladden things, fire and marsh have no part in it—it is spirit. As for water, I know that it moistens things; as for Gen [mountain], I know that it brings things to completion and initiates their beginning. Yet as for that whereby they moisten and whereby they complete and initiate things, Kan [water] and Gen have no part in it—it is spirit. Each dedicates itself to a single aspect of generation and completion, yet the indwelling master is unfathomable in its function; is this not what is meant by "spirit wondrously working through the myriad things"? Yet as for the transformations and changes of these six offspring-trigrams, how could they operate of their own accord? And as for the completion of things, how could they come to completion of their own accord? When I observe the hexagrams of the Former Heaven [Fuxi's arrangement], water and fire reach one another, thunder and wind do not conflict with one another, mountain and marsh communicate their vital breath, and that which divides yin and divides yang conceals itself in its abode. Thus it is that in the wake of alternation and transformation, things attain their moistening and drying, things attain their stirring and bending, and things attain their gladdening and completion, while that which is rooted in yin and rooted in yang makes wondrous its achievement. Therefore, change is nothing other than yin uniting with yang and only then changing; transformation is nothing other than yang uniting with yin and only then transforming; completion is nothing other than yin and yang depending on one another and thus coming to completion. Hence, when one observes the trigrams of the Former Heaven and the Later Heaven [King Wen's arrangement], spirit and transformation are united, and substance and function are complete. Broadly speaking, spirit governs physical form; that spirit presides over ease while form bears the toil is the distinction between movement and stillness. In the Later Heaven arrangement, the Sage retired the two parents [Qian and Kun] from active use, while generation, overcoming, succession, and continuation each follow its proper season—all of which is simply the means to honor the Way of spirit. Alas! The spirit of creation is ever attained through stillness, whereas the spirit of the human mind is ever lost …

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
於動奈之何其不思
書
后非民罔使民非后罔事無自廣以狹人
匹夫匹婦不獲自盡民主罔與成厥功
余鏜
同考試官訓導楊批詞理俱精而說無自廣
狹人處更有關係可錄
同考試官敎諭姜批就題發揮無一字不精
到
===
考試官敎諭胡批構詞命意迥異衆作
考試官敎諭陳批得伊尹告君之意
大臣論君民相須而欲取善廣其量焉夫人君
合天下以成其善也知君民之相須而取善可
有遺乎且人君非一人之身也聖德非一善之
積也盍觀君民之際乎彼君使人者也非民則
孰與奉一人之役是君不可無民也民事人者
也非君則孰與統萬姓之心是民不可無君也
故庶民之論議雖微而有可採一己之聰明雖
punctuated:
於動，奈之何其不思？

《書》
「后非民罔使，民非后罔事。無自廣以狹人，匹夫匹婦不獲自盡，民主罔與成厥功。」
余鏜
同考試官訓導楊批：詞理俱精，而說「無自廣狹人」處更有關係，可錄。
同考試官敎諭姜批：就題發揮，無一字不精到。
考試官敎諭胡批：構詞命意，迥異衆作。
考試官敎諭陳批：得伊尹告君之意。

大臣論君民相須，而欲取善廣其量焉。夫人君合天下以成其善也，知君民之相須，而取善可有遺乎？且人君非一人之身也，聖德非一善之積也，盍觀君民之際乎？彼君，使人者也，非民則孰與奉一人之役？是君不可無民也。民，事人者也，非君則孰與統萬姓之心？是民不可無君也。故庶民之論議雖微而有可採，一己之聰明雖
translation_en:
… in movement. How can one fail to reflect on this?

Classic of Documents (Shu)
"The sovereign without the people has none whom he can employ; and the people without the sovereign have none whom they can serve. Do not think yourself so large as to deem others small. If ordinary men and women do not find the opportunity to give full development to their ability, the people's lord will be without those with whom to complete his merit."
Yu Tang 余鏜
Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Yang comments: Both the diction and the reasoning are refined, and the explanation of the passage "do not think yourself so large as to deem others small" is of even greater import; it is worthy of selection.
Associate Examiner Instructor Jiang comments: Expounding closely upon the topic, there is not a single word that fails to hit the mark with precision.
Examiner Instructor Hu comments: Its phrasing and conception are vastly superior to the common run of compositions.
Examiner Instructor Chen comments: It captures the true intent of Yi Yin's 伊尹 admonition to his ruler.

The great minister discusses the mutual dependence of sovereign and people, desiring that in adopting what is good, the ruler should broaden his capacity. Now, the ruler of men brings together the whole realm in order to perfect his goodness; knowing the mutual dependence of sovereign and people, how could anything be overlooked in adopting what is good? Moreover, the ruler of men does not consist merely of a single person's body, nor is sage virtue the accumulation of a single good deed. Why not observe the relationship between sovereign and people? That sovereign is one who employs others; without the people, who would perform the service due to the One Man? Thus the sovereign cannot be without the people. The people are those who serve others; without the sovereign, who would unite the hearts of the myriad surnames? Thus the people cannot be without the sovereign. Therefore, although the discussions and deliberations of the common people are humble, they contain what is worth adopting; although one's own intelligence and acuity are …

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
高而不可恃寧以聖人而擇芻蕘之言也毋自
廣其能而狹人之能也寧以天子而納閭閻之
慮也毋自廣其善而狹人之善也何也生一自
廣之心則何德非已存一狹人之念則何人有
德忠智之謨且阻于千里之外矣夫婦之愚安
能自效乎師保之訓且塞于九陛之下矣夫婦
之賤安能自達乎雖匹夫匹婦之善未必裨于
天子之聖明而一言一善之遺終有虧於聖人
之光大何自而成厥功耶信乎聖德無可滿之
===
量而庶官左右之外尤有不盡之師也人君可
不合天下以成其善哉嗟乎人君之最患莫大
乎有已彼天之所大奉左右所從臾巍然自視
不勝其廣舉天下莫與比智而較能夫惟心虛
則萬善皆入而可以倂包天下故堯稱大哉以
其能舍已也此一德之本也
太史司寇蘇公式敬爾由獄以長我王國
茲式有慎以列用中罰
黃仕鳳
punctuated:
高，而不可恃。寧以聖人而擇芻蕘之言也，毋自廣其能而狹人之能也；寧以天子而納閭閻之慮也，毋自廣其善而狹人之善也。何也？生一自廣之心，則何德非已？存一狹人之念，則何人有德？忠智之謨，且阻于千里之外矣，夫婦之愚，安能自效乎？師保之訓，且塞于九陛之下矣，夫婦之賤，安能自達乎？雖匹夫匹婦之善，未必裨于天子之聖明，而一言一善之遺，終有虧於聖人之光大，何自而成厥功耶？信乎聖德無可滿之量，而庶官左右之外，尤有不盡之師也。人君可不合天下以成其善哉？嗟乎！人君之最患，莫大乎有已。彼天之所大奉，左右所從臾，巍然自視，不勝其廣，舉天下莫與比智而較能。夫惟心虛，則萬善皆入，而可以倂包天下。故堯稱「大哉」，以其能舍已也。此一德之本也。

太史、司寇蘇公，式敬爾由獄，以長我王國。茲式有慎，以列用中罰。
黃仕鳳
translation_en:
… lofty, it cannot be relied upon. Rather than magnifying one's own abilities and belittling the abilities of others, it is better, though a sage, to select from the words of grass-cutters and firewood-gatherers; rather than magnifying one's own goodness and belittling the goodness of others, it is better, though the Son of Heaven, to accept the deliberations of the village lanes. Why is this? If one gives rise to a mind that magnifies oneself, then what virtue will not be deemed already one's own? If one harbors a thought that belittles others, then what other person will be deemed to possess virtue? When the counsels of the loyal and wise are blocked a thousand li away, how can the ignorance of ordinary men and women offer its service? When the instructions of tutors and guardians are obstructed below the nine steps of the throne, how can the lowliness of ordinary men and women make itself heard? Although the goodness of a common man or woman may not necessarily add to the sagely intelligence of the Son of Heaven, the omission of a single word or a single good deed ultimately detracts from the glorious greatness of a sage—how then could he accomplish his achievements? Truly, sagely virtue has a capacity that can never be filled to satisfaction, and beyond the multitude of officials and royal attendants, there are still inexhaustible teachers. How can a ruler not unite the whole world to bring his goodness to completion? Alas! The greatest affliction of a ruler is none greater than being full of himself. Greatly favored by Heaven and urged on by his attendants, he regards himself loftily and feels boundlessly expansive, supposing that in the entire world none can compare with his wisdom or rival his ability. Yet only when the mind is humble can ten thousand virtues enter in, allowing him to encompass the entire world. Therefore Yao was praised as "Great indeed!" because he was able to set aside himself. This is the foundation of pure and constant virtue.

"The Grand Scribe and the Minister of Crime, Duke Su, was reverent in the judicial cases he handled, thereby perpetuating our royal state. Herein take your model with caution, so as to array and apply the just punishments." [Book of Documents, "Lizheng"]
Huang Shifeng 黃仕鳳

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導楊批訓旨精透發周公倦倦
慎獄之意盎然當是作者
同考試官教諭姜批發意明悉措語鏗鏘是
邃於經學者
考試官教諭胡批朗然可誦
考試官教諭陳批有藻思
大臣告太史欲以祥刑而垂憲焉蓋祥刑垂憲
萬世也蘇公以之太史可無書乎周公若曰刑
之所係大矣用之得人則以刑壽國用之匪人
===
則以刑病國爾太史其知哲人之刑乎彼司寇
蘇公之掌邦禁也一輕一重悉裁之於敬惕乎
天命之嚴一取一舍悉歸之於敬凜乎民情之
畏式敬爾由獄焉敬至則刑不濫而四海之大
命以立社稷有道之長若或延之也刑清則世
自泰而一代之元氣以培國家不拔之基若或
固之也用罰至是無乎不愼無乎不中而可爲
後世式矣爾其書之史焉俾嗣公而興者心公
之心典公之獄者法公之法輕之不可重之不
punctuated:
同考試官訓導楊批：訓旨精透，發周公倦倦慎獄之意盎然，當是作者。
同考試官教諭姜批：發意明悉，措語鏗鏘，是邃於經學者。
考試官教諭胡批：朗然可誦。
考試官教諭陳批：有藻思。
大臣告太史，欲以祥刑而垂憲焉。蓋祥刑垂憲萬世也，蘇公以之，太史可無書乎？周公若曰：刑之所係大矣！用之得人，則以刑壽國；用之匪人，則以刑病國。爾太史其知哲人之刑乎？彼司寇蘇公之掌邦禁也，一輕一重，悉裁之於敬，惕乎天命之嚴；一取一舍，悉歸之於敬，凜乎民情之畏，式敬爾由獄焉。敬至則刑不濫，而四海之大命以立，社稷有道之長，若或延之也；刑清則世自泰，而一代之元氣以培，國家不拔之基，若或固之也。用罰至是，無乎不愼，無乎不中，而可爲後世式矣！爾其書之史焉，俾嗣公而興者心公之心，典公之獄者法公之法。輕之不可，重之不
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Yang: The exposition of the purport is precise and penetrating, richly bringing out the Duke of Zhou's earnest intent to be cautious in judicial cases; he must be a master writer.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Jiang: The expression of the meaning is clear and thorough, and the phrasing is resonant and forceful; he is one deeply versed in classical learning.
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Hu: Clear and worthy of recitation.
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Chen: Possesses refined literary thought.
The great minister addresses the Grand Scribe, wishing to hand down a model through auspicious punishments. Indeed, auspicious punishments serve to hand down a model for ten thousand generations; since Duke Su practiced this, how could the Grand Scribe fail to record it? It is as if the Duke of Zhou said: What depends upon punishments is great indeed! When their administration is entrusted to the right person, punishments prolong the life of the state; when entrusted to the wrong person, punishments harm the state. Do you, Grand Scribe, understand the punishments of a wise man? When that Minister of Crime, Duke Su, took charge of the state's prohibitions, every leniency and every severity was wholly decided out of reverence, standing in awe of the strictness of the Mandate of Heaven; every conviction and every release was wholly rooted in reverence, trembling before the fearfulness of the people's sentiments—thus showing reverence in the judicial cases he handled. When reverence reaches the utmost, punishments are not excessive,whereby the great destiny of the Four Seas is established, and the enduring longevity of a principled state is as though prolonged by it; when punishments are pure, the age is naturally at peace, whereby the vital energy of a generation is nurtured, and the unshakable foundation of the dynastic state is as though consolidated by it. When the application of penalties reaches this point, there is nothing in which it is not cautious, nothing in which it is not balanced, so that it can serve as a model for later generations! You shall record this in the histories, causing those who rise up to succeed the Duke to take the Duke's mind as their own mind, and those who take charge of the Duke's judicial cases to take the Duke's law as their model. To make them too light will not do, and to make them too heavy will not…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
可而輕重之間有中在也昭乎成憲之如新式
而用之爲天下持平而已矣取之不得舍之不
得而取舍之間有中在也秩然令章之咸具式
而用之爲朝廷執法而已矣敬獄之風異人如
一心而王國之長亦萬年如一日也哉吁用獄
敬則刑罰中紀載公則垂示遠周公旣以誤獄
戒成王而復以敬獄告太史其爲周家之慮深
哉蓋聞虞廷恤刑欽哉是勅夫敬所以制中也
爲民司命敢不敬與穆王荒耄猶曰何敬非刑
===
具嚴天威豈太史之書司寇之式有以啓之然
訓祥刑而列罰鍰何屑屑焉故下式敬而上罔
知體也
詩
菁菁者莪在彼中沚旣見君子我心則喜
黃維貴
同考試官敎諭姚批發我心喜處透徹而精
采燁如
同考試官敎諭高批詞俊調高理明意婉詩
punctuated:
可，而輕重之間有中在也。昭乎成憲之如新，式而用之，爲天下持平而已矣。取之不得，舍之不得，而取舍之間有中在也。秩然令章之咸具，式而用之，爲朝廷執法而已矣。敬獄之風，異人如一心；而王國之長，亦萬年如一日也哉！吁，用獄敬則刑罰中，紀載公則垂示遠。周公旣以誤獄戒成王，而復以敬獄告太史，其爲周家之慮深哉！蓋聞虞廷恤刑，欽哉是勅。夫敬，所以制中也。爲民司命，敢不敬與？穆王荒耄，猶曰：「何敬非刑，具嚴天威。」豈太史之書、司寇之式有以啓之？然訓祥刑而列罰鍰，何屑屑焉！故下式敬，而上罔知體也。

詩
菁菁者莪，在彼中沚。旣見君子，我心則喜。
黃維貴
同考試官敎諭姚批：發「我心喜」處透徹，而精采燁如。
同考試官敎諭高批：詞俊調高，理明意婉，詩…
translation_en:
… nor make them heavier, for between lightness and heaviness lies the mean. Brightly, the established constitutions remain as if new; taking them as a model and applying them is simply to maintain fairness for the world. They will not be able to accept or reject arbitrarily, for between acceptance and rejection lies the mean. Orderly, the fine statutes are all complete; taking them as a model and applying them is simply to uphold the law for the court. When the custom of approaching litigation with reverence unites different men as if of one mind, the longevity of the royal state will likewise endure for ten thousand years as if a single day! Ah, when litigation is handled with reverence, punishments hit the mark; when historical records are impartial, their instruction reaches far into the future. Having warned King Cheng against miscarriages of justice, the Duke of Zhou again instructed the Grand Scribe on reverence in litigation—how deep was his concern for the House of Zhou! Indeed, we hear that when the court of Yu showed compassion in punishment, its charge was "Be reverent!" For reverence is the means by which the mean is attained. As those who hold the命 (lives) of the people in their hands, how dare they not be reverent? Even when King Mu was in his senile dotage, he still said, "What should you revere if not punishments? Together hold in awe the majesty of Heaven." Could it be that the writings of the Grand Scribe and the model of the Minister of Crime (sikou) inspired him? Yet in teaching auspicious punishments and listing redemption fines in metal, how petty and trifling he was! Thus those below took reverence as their model, while the sovereign above failed to grasp the essential principle.

Book of Odes (Shi)
"Luxuriant is the tarragon, there in the midst of the islet. Having seen the noble man, my heart is delighted."
By Huang Weigui 黃維貴
Associate Examiner and Instructor Yao comments: It thoroughly brings out the meaning of "my heart is delighted," and its brilliance shines forth.
Associate Examiner and Instructor Gao comments: The diction is refined and the tone lofty, the reasoning clear and the meaning subtle; among essays on the Book of Odes…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
義上乘也
考試官敎諭胡批以有儀來形心喜最妙
考試官敎諭陳批題淡而文有味
詩人興已之見賢而誠於喜焉夫喜出于心其
喜也誠矣詩人以之眞能悅賢者哉歌菁莪者
意謂見賢而喜者情也顧儀弗備則簡心弗至
則虛今之樂且有儀豈飾喜哉彼莪之菁菁而
盛也中沚在焉是物且因地而適矣况見君子
而喜也有不由于心乎吾知方其未見也仰而
===
思思而憂吾之精神先與君子相爲流通及今
既見也遇斯喜喜斯陶吾之意氣自與君子相
爲浹洽喜起形于一堂匪迹也本吾中心好之
者爲社稷慶也慶歸社稷喜出吾心殆舉其素
所蘊結于衷者而盡宣之矣笑語形於九陛匪
文也本吾心乎愛之者爲生民幸也幸在生民
喜自吾心殆舉其素所抑鬱于衷者而盡暢之
矣是蓋鐘鼓載陳喜之聲也玉帛交錯喜之容
也於聲容而樂之其心猶有未慊式燕未舉心
punctuated:
義上乘也。
考試官敎諭胡批：以有儀來形心喜，最妙。
考試官敎諭陳批：題淡而文有味。
詩人興已之見賢，而誠於喜焉。夫喜出于心，其喜也誠矣。詩人以之，眞能悅賢者哉！歌《菁莪》者，意謂：見賢而喜者，情也；顧儀弗備則簡，心弗至則虛。今之「樂且有儀」，豈飾喜哉？彼莪之菁菁而盛也，中沚在焉，是物且因地而適矣，况見君子而喜也，有不由于心乎？吾知方其未見也，仰而思，思而憂，吾之精神先與君子相爲流通；及今既見也，遇斯喜，喜斯陶，吾之意氣自與君子相爲浹洽。喜起形于一堂，匪迹也，本吾中心好之者，爲社稷慶也；慶歸社稷，喜出吾心，殆舉其素所蘊結于衷者而盡宣之矣。笑語形於九陛，匪文也，本吾心乎愛之者，爲生民幸也；幸在生民，喜自吾心，殆舉其素所抑鬱于衷者而盡暢之矣。是蓋鐘鼓載陳，喜之聲也；玉帛交錯，喜之容也。於聲容而樂之，其心猶有未慊；式燕未舉，心
translation_en:
…is a first-rate essay on the Classic of Poetry.
Examiner Instructor Hu commented: Using the subsequent line "with proper ceremony" to bring out the joy in the heart is most marvelous.
Examiner Instructor Chen commented: The topic is plain, yet the essay is full of flavor.

The poet uses an evocative image to express his seeing men of worth and feeling sincere joy therein. Now, when joy issues from the heart, that joy is sincere indeed. Taking this to heart, the poet was truly one who could delight in men of worth! The meaning of the one who sang "Lush is the Tarragon" (Jing'e) is this: to rejoice upon seeing men of worth is a natural feeling; yet if ceremony is not complete, it is negligent, and if the heart is not fully present, it is hollow. When the ode goes on to say "delighted and with proper ceremony," how could that merely be a feigned display of joy? Look at that tarragon growing so lush and luxuriant: it is there in the midst of the islet. Even such a plant finds contentment according to its place; how much more so, when one rejoices upon seeing a noble man, could that fail to issue from the heart?

I know that before he has seen him, he looks up and longs for him, and longing, feels anxious—his spirit already communicates back and forth with the noble man beforehand. And now, having seen him, meeting brings joy, and joy brings elation—his spirit and disposition naturally blend in harmony with the noble man. Joyous exultation takes form in the single hall, yet it is not mere outward trace: rooted in the fondness at the core of my heart, it is a celebration for the altars of state. While the celebration belongs to the altars of state, the joy issues from my heart, well-nigh taking all that had long been pent up within my breast and giving it complete expression. Laughter and converse take form upon the nine steps of the throne, yet it is not mere outward ornament: rooted in the love within my heart, it is good fortune for the common people. While the good fortune rests with the common people, the joy comes from my heart, well-nigh taking all that had long been suppressed within my breast and giving it complete release.

Thus, the setting out of bells and drums is the sound of joy; the crisscrossing of jades and silks is the demeanor of joy. Were one to take delight only in sounds and demeanor, the heart would still remain unsatisfied. Before the feast is even held, the heart…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
先和也幣帛未將心先獻也於根心而喜之其
儀始爲不虛吁菁莪詩人眞篤于好賢矣甞觀
明良感召如宮應而角動由心先之故不介而
親也若儀不及物賢者豈虛拘哉然隰桑亦好
賢也惟欲其心之不謂不忘而是詩播之詠歌
彰之儀物若亟于自見其心何哉蓋隰桑喜見
欲心之藏于已菁莪燕賓欲心之達于人豈好
之有淺深耶
干祿百福子孫千億穆穆皇皇宜君宜王
===
不愆不忘率由舊章
王家相
同考試官教諭姚批以俊雅之詞發微婉之
趣鏘鏘乎明堂遺響矣
同考試官教諭高批頌美得體鋪敘有法令
人讀之不能釋手
考試官教諭胡批得頌不忘規意
考試官教諭陳批詞莊而麗
詩願王者之福惟後胤之多賢也蓋王者以後
punctuated:
先和也，幣帛未將，心先獻也。於根心而喜之，其儀始爲不虛。吁！《菁莪》詩人眞篤于好賢矣。甞觀明良感召，如宮應而角動，由心先之，故不介而親也。若儀不及物，賢者豈虛拘哉？然《隰桑》亦好賢也，惟欲其心之不謂不忘，而是詩播之詠歌，彰之儀物，若亟于自見其心，何哉？蓋《隰桑》喜見，欲心之藏于已；《菁莪》燕賓，欲心之達于人，豈好之有淺深耶？

「干祿百福，子孫千億。穆穆皇皇，宜君宜王。不愆不忘，率由舊章。」
王家相
同考試官教諭姚批：以俊雅之詞，發微婉之趣，鏘鏘乎明堂遺響矣。
同考試官教諭高批：頌美得體，鋪敘有法，令人讀之不能釋手。
考試官教諭胡批：得頌不忘規意。
考試官教諭陳批：詞莊而麗。

詩願王者之福，惟後胤之多賢也。蓋王者以後
translation_en:
… is already in harmony; before the silk gifts are presented, the heart has already made its offering. Only when the joy springs from the root of the heart does the ceremony become truly genuine. Ah! The poet of "Luxuriant Tarragon" (Jing'e) was truly sincere in loving the worthy! When we observe the mutual resonance between an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers, it is like the gong note answering and the jue note vibrating—because the heart leads the way, they become close without an intermediary. If the ceremony does not match the material gifts, how could worthy men be detained by empty forms? Yet the ode "Lowland Mulberry" (Xisang) also expresses love for the worthy, wishing only not to speak of it and never to forget it in the heart; whereas this ode broadcasts it in song and displays it in ceremonial gifts, as if eager to reveal its own heart—why is that? It is because "Lowland Mulberry" rejoices in seeing the worthy and wishes the feeling to be treasured within oneself, whereas "Luxuriant Tarragon" feasts the guests and wishes the feeling to be communicated to others. How could there be any difference in the depth of their affection?

"Seeking blessings and a hundred felicities, may his sons and grandsons be a thousand, a hundred million! August and majestic, fit to be lord, fit to be king; neither erring nor forgetting, following the old statutes."
By Wang Jiaxiang.
Associate Examiner Instructor Yao comments: Using refined and elegant diction to bring out subtle and gentle nuances, it resonates with the lingering echoes of the Hall of Light!
Associate Examiner Instructor Gao comments: The eulogy is fitting and the exposition well-structured; reading it, one cannot put it down.
Examiner Instructor Hu comments: It captures the spirit of offering praise without forgetting admonition.
Examiner Instructor Chen comments: The language is dignified and resplendent.

The ode wishes for the king's blessing to consist solely in having numerous and worthy descendants. For a true king takes his posterity…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
胤為福也多而且賢百福孰大于是想其答君
貺若曰天下惟有道之君為能集昌後之福故
帝王之享有全福每於後嗣徵之也王之福何
如哉吾知顯德在王其干祿也有道百福在天
其申錫也無窮福王之子而子以千億天若為
宗社而發其祥福王之孫而孫以千億天若為
邦家而衍其慶然非徒多而已也貞元會合則
賢聖繼出莫不穆穆焉皇皇焉王有世德而子
孫皆象賢也大德得位則君王聖明莫不宜君
===
焉宜王焉王有世業而子孫皆勝任也攄敬美
之猷豈不能更一法制哉過之不敢忘之不敢
惟知我周有家法在焉吾為先王守之而已矣
撫君王之位豈不能作一聰明哉無敢過越無
敢遺忘惟知我周有祖訓在焉吾為先王率之
而已矣蓋周官洛誥之貽本為萬世之君王而
立極善繼善述之道遂合千億之子孫而共由
至是則帝王之統有託而明聖之緒不患無傳
矣百福其遠哉嘗觀創業之君憂深思遠其法
punctuated: 胤為福也，多而且賢，百福孰大于是？想其答君貺，若曰：天下惟有道之君，為能集昌後之福，故帝王之享有全福，每於後嗣徵之也。王之福何如哉？吾知顯德在王，其干祿也有道；百福在天，其申錫也無窮。福王之子，而子以千億，天若為宗社而發其祥；福王之孫，而孫以千億，天若為邦家而衍其慶。然非徒多而已也。貞元會合，則賢聖繼出，莫不穆穆焉、皇皇焉，王有世德，而子孫皆象賢也；大德得位，則君王聖明，莫不宜君焉、宜王焉，王有世業，而子孫皆勝任也。攄敬美之猷，豈不能更一法制哉？過之不敢，忘之不敢，惟知我周有家法在焉，吾為先王守之而已矣；撫君王之位，豈不能作一聰明哉？無敢過越，無敢遺忘，惟知我周有祖訓在焉，吾為先王率之而已矣。蓋《周官》、《洛誥》之貽，本為萬世之君王而立極；善繼善述之道，遂合千億之子孫而共由。至是，則帝王之統有託，而明聖之緒不患無傳矣，百福其遠哉！嘗觀創業之君，憂深思遠，其法
translation_en: … posterity to be his blessing; when they are both numerous and worthy, which of the hundred blessings is greater than this? Imagining how the ode responds to the ruler's favors, it is as if to say: In all under Heaven, only a ruler who possesses the Way is able to gather the blessing of flourishing descendants; therefore, an emperor's or king's enjoyment of complete blessing is always verified in his heirs. What is the King's blessing like? I know that illustrious virtue resides in the King, and his seeking of禄 [emolument/blessing] follows the Way; the hundred blessings reside in Heaven, and its repeated bestowals are inexhaustible. It blesses the King's sons, so his sons number in the thousands and hundreds of thousands, as though Heaven were bringing forth auspiciousness for the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain; it blesses the King's grandsons, so his grandsons number in the thousands and hundreds of thousands, as though Heaven were extending felicity for the state and royal house. Yet they are not merely numerous! When the cosmic cycles of Zhen and Yuan converge, worthies and sages emerge in succession: none is not reverent and august, none is not splendid and majestic; the King possesses hereditary virtue, and his sons and grandsons all emulate the worthy. When great virtue attains the throne, the rulers and kings are sage and enlightened: none is notfit to be ruler, none is not fit to be king; the King possesses a hereditary enterprise, and his sons and grandsons are all equal to the responsibility. In unfolding their reverent and admirable counsels, how could they not alter a single law or institution? Yet they dare not overstep them, and they dare not forget them; they know only that our Zhou possesses its family laws, and say, "We simply guard them on behalf of the former kings." In occupying the position of ruler and king, how could they not exercise some cleverness of their own? Yet they dare not transgress, and they dare not neglect; they know only that our Zhou possesses its ancestral instructions, and say, "We simply follow them on behalf of the former kings." Indeed, the legacies bequeathed in the Offices of Zhou (Zhou guan) and the Announcement Concerning Luo (Luo gao) originally established the supreme standard for rulers and kings of ten thousand generations; the Way of skillfully continuing the will and skillfully carrying forward the affairs of one's predecessors thus unites thousands and hundreds of thousands of sons and grandsons in following the same path together. When it reaches this point, the line of emperors and kings has those to whom it can be entrusted, and there is no worry that the thread of enlightened sages will lack transmission—how far-reaching are the hundred blessings! I have observed that rulers who found a dynasty have deep concerns and far-reaching thoughts; their laws…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
足垂永久而好大者恥循習喜事者樂紛更非
福也故以旦之臣輔成之君取其舊而盡更之
何難哉尚曰儀刑文王則知敬美不足恃而成
憲所當遵也是詩其有周公之忠愛耶
春秋
八月公會齊侯宋公鄭伯曹伯邾人于檉〔僖公元年〕秋齊侯宋公江人黃人會于
陽穀〔僖公三年〕遂伐楚次于陘楚屈
完來盟于師盟于召陵〔俱僖公四年〕
===
張萱
同考試官訓導鄭批〔比屬端整而不分愈深禮謹最得傳旨〕
考試官敎諭胡批〔形容桓伯帖楚意殆盡〕
考試官敎諭陳批〔森然得體〕
春秋紀伯主憂外有善于制之者有善于服之
者此桓之制楚服楚則能憂之效也且善始者
不必善終自昔記之迺有以識明之主才優之
臣而不克持其終者非其初然也方楚之未帖
punctuated:
足垂永久，而好大者恥循習，喜事者樂紛更，非福也。故以旦之臣，輔成之君，取其舊而盡更之，何難哉？尚曰「儀刑文王」，則知敬美不足恃，而成憲所當遵也。是詩其有周公之忠愛耶！

《春秋》
「八月，公會齊侯、宋公、鄭伯、曹伯、邾人于檉」〔僖公元年〕，「秋，齊侯、宋公、江人、黃人會于陽穀」〔僖公三年〕，「遂伐楚，次于陘，楚屈完來盟于師，盟于召陵」〔俱僖公四年〕。

張萱
同考試官訓導鄭批：〔比屬端整，而不分愈深，禮謹，最得傳旨。〕
考試官敎諭胡批：〔形容桓伯帖楚意殆盡。〕
考試官敎諭陳批：〔森然得體。〕

《春秋》紀伯主憂外，有善于制之者，有善于服之者。此桓之制楚、服楚，則能憂之效也。且善始者不必善終，自昔記之。迺有以識明之主、才優之臣，而不克持其終者，非其初然也。方楚之未帖，
translation_en:
… suffice to be handed down for perpetuity; yet those who are fond of grandiose schemes are ashamed to follow established practice, and those who delight in meddling take pleasure in reckless alterations—this is not a blessing. Therefore, with a minister like Dan [the Duke of Zhou] assisting a sovereign like King Cheng, what difficulty would there have been in taking the old institutions and completely changing them? Yet it still says, "Take King Wen as your model," from which we know that one's own reverent virtue and fine qualities are not enough to rely upon, and that the established statutes are what must be followed. Does this ode not embody the loyal devotion of the Duke of Zhou!

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)
"In the eighth month, the Duke met the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, and a man of Zhu at Cheng" [1st year of Duke Xi]; "In autumn, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, a man of Jiang, and a man of Huang met at Yanggu" [3rd year of Duke Xi]; "Thereupon they invaded Chu and halted at Xing. Qu Wan of Chu came to the army to make a covenant, and they covenanted at Shaoling" [all 4th year of Duke Xi].

Zhang Xuan 张萱
Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Zheng comments: [The pairing of events is neat and orderly, and by not dividing them the meaning grows ever deeper; the ritual propriety is严谨 (rigorous), best capturing the purport of the commentary.]
Examiner, Instructor Hu comments: [Depicts Hegemon Huan's intent in subduing Chu almost exhaustively.]
Examiner, Instructor Chen comments: [Majestic and well-proportioned.]

When the Spring and Autumn Annals records how a hegemon-lord was concerned about external threats, there was skill in keeping them in check, and there was skill in bringing them to submission. Here, Duke Huan's checking of Chu and bringing Chu to submission were the effects of his ability to take concern. Moreover, that those who begin well do not necessarily end well has been recorded since antiquity. Yet when a sovereign of clear insight and a minister of superior talent are unable to sustain things to the end, it was not so for them at the beginning. Just when Chu had not yet been subdued…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
而桓仲憂之以爲楚之伺釁而動寔甞我威而
江黃新服用□爲齊不用則楚其信不可失也
故檉會而鄭勤矣陽穀會而伐楚謀矣樽俎折
衝方行華裔而加之與國之援其威內振其信
外孚將無俟撻伐一加而溱洧以南漢陽以東
悉就齊之畫中矣又以楚之逆師問故寔觀我
詞而屈完來款以德則服以衆則難其禮不可
失也故陘次而包茅問矣召陵退而盟禮成矣
文告威讓氣奪强敵而加之先好之徵其詞順
===
其禮恭將無俟攻戰爲威而方城之城漢水之
池悉安齊之宇下矣夫以桓仲之憂楚而思屈
其力也如是思屈其心也如是慮其勝而持其
勝也又如是其爲念一何深而爲禮一何謹也
此無異故焉方憂之君不必王德而可與慮危
方憂之臣不必王佐而可與圖艱也楚帖而志
驕志驕而行肆陳之討遂紛紛矣攷桓仲之初
決策也固曰速得志於天下諸侯夫桓之得志
孰踰召陵者故桓仲之驕溢召陵以前爲之也
punctuated: 而桓、仲憂之，以爲楚之伺釁而動，寔甞我威；而江、黃新服，用□爲齊，不用則楚，其信不可失也。故檉會而鄭勤矣，陽穀會而伐楚謀矣。樽俎折衝，方行華裔，而加之與國之援，其威內振，其信外孚，將無俟撻伐一加，而溱、洧以南，漢陽以東，悉就齊之畫中矣。又以楚之逆師問故，寔觀我詞；而屈完來款，以德則服，以衆則難，其禮不可失也。故陘次而包茅問矣，召陵退而盟禮成矣。文告威讓，氣奪强敵，而加之先好之徵，其詞順，其禮恭，將無俟攻戰爲威，而方城之城，漢水之池，悉安齊之宇下矣。夫以桓、仲之憂楚，而思屈其力也如是，思屈其心也如是，慮其勝而持其勝也又如是，其爲念一何深，而爲禮一何謹也！此無異故焉，方憂之君，不必王德而可與慮危；方憂之臣，不必王佐而可與圖艱也。楚帖而志驕，志驕而行肆，陳之討遂紛紛矣。攷桓、仲之初決策也，固曰速得志於天下諸侯。夫桓之得志，孰踰召陵者？故桓、仲之驕溢，召陵以前爲之也。
translation_en:
…and Duke Huan and Guan Zhong 管仲 worried about it. They considered that Chu’s watching for an opening to act was truly testing our prestige; and as Jiang and Huang had newly submitted, if employed [they would] be for Qi, whereas if not employed they would go over to Chu—so good faith with them could not be lost. Therefore, at the meeting at Cheng, Zheng was diligently attended to; and at the meeting at Yanggu, the campaign against Chu was planned. Subduing the enemy over ritual vessels and sacrificial stands was just then being carried out among the Chinese states and outer tribes, and when there was added to this the support of allied states, his prestige stirred those within and his good faith inspired confidence without. Even before waiting to launch a single punitive strike, everything south of the Zhen and Wei rivers and east of Hanyang had already fallen into Qi’s grand design.

They also considered that when Chu met the army to ask the reason for the incursion, it was truly observing our rhetoric; and when Qu Wan 屈完 came to seek terms, by virtue they would submit, whereas by force of numbers it would be difficult—so propriety toward them could not be lost. Therefore, halting at Xing, the tribute of wrapped rush-grass was demanded; and retreating to Shaoling, the rites of the covenant were completed. Through written proclamations and stern reproofs, the spirit of a powerful enemy was overawed, and when there was added to this the invocation of former amity, his words were compliant and his rites respectful. Even before waiting to establish prestige through assault and battle, the walls of Fangcheng and the moat of the Han River were all at peace beneath the shelter of Qi.

Now, considering how Duke Huan and Guan Zhong worried about Chu—how they sought to subdue its strength like this, how they sought to subdue its heart like this, and how they planned for victory and maintained that victory like this—how deep was their forethought, and how cautious their propriety! There is no other reason for this: a ruler in the midst of worry need not possess kingly virtue to be someone with whom one can take precautions against peril; a minister in the midst of worry need not be a kingly coadjutor to be someone with whom one can plan against hardship. Once Chu was subdued, their ambitions grew arrogant; once their ambitions grew arrogant, their conduct became unrestrained, and the punitive expeditions against Chen subsequently fell into disorder. If we examine the initial decision on strategy by Duke Huan and Guan Zhong, they indeed spoke of quickly realizing their ambitions among the feudal lords of the world. Now, in Duke Huan’s realization of his ambitions, what surpassed Shaoling? Therefore, the arrogance and excess of Duke Huan and Guan Zhong were already formed prior to Shaoling.

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
公會晉侯宋公陳侯衛侯鄭伯曹伯莒子
邾子滕子薛伯齊世子光吳人鄫人于
戚〔襄公五年〕
張萃
同考試官訓導鄭批〔傳中來會說是不為主〕
此作發揮有思
考試官教諭胡批〔融會二傳成文可誦〕
考試官教諭陳批〔得進吳意〕
春秋于遠人與好而特進其慕義焉此吳之慕
===
義而聽命於戚異乎夷矣欲無進之得乎昔于
戚之會吳以人稱我無所貶而彼焉可會何也
夫自伐郯以還而諸侯俛首於北吳人雄視於
東者逾十餘年而悼也賢伯也通吳以制楚義
舉也彼雖僭號之夷乃其慕我華風也甚堅而
欲從事於會也甚切是故悔淮上之不至而遣
壽越以求通也則曰寡君願徼福于唐叔二文
奉贄幣以見于君惟不虞之不戒以至失時寡
君敢伏其辜感善道之為期而煩魯衛以告虔
punctuated:
「公會晉侯、宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、曹伯、莒子、邾子、滕子、薛伯、齊世子光、吳人、鄫人于戚。」〔襄公五年〕

張萃

同考試官訓導鄭批：〔傳中「來會」說，是不為主。〕此作發揮有思。
考試官教諭胡批：〔融會二傳成文，可誦。〕
考試官教諭陳批：〔得進吳意。〕

《春秋》于遠人與好，而特進其慕義焉。此吳之慕義而聽命於戚，異乎夷矣，欲無進之，得乎？昔于戚之會，吳以「人」稱，我無所貶，而彼焉可會，何也？夫自伐郯以還，而諸侯俛首於北，吳人雄視於東者逾十餘年；而悼也，賢伯也，通吳以制楚，義舉也。彼雖僭號之夷，乃其慕我華風也甚堅，而欲從事於會也甚切。是故悔淮上之不至，而遣壽越以求通也，則曰：「寡君願徼福于唐叔、二文，奉贄幣以見于君；惟不虞之不戒，以至失時，寡君敢伏其辜。」感善道之為期，而煩魯、衛以告虔…
translation_en:
"The Duke met the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, Heir Apparent Guang of Qi, a man of Wu, and a man of Zeng at Qi." [Fifth Year of Duke Xiang]

Zhang Cui 

Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Zheng comments: [The explanation of "coming to the meeting" in the commentary means that Wu did not act as the host.] This composition develops the theme thoughtfully.
Examiner and Instructor Hu comments: [It synthesizes two commentaries into a well-crafted essay worth reciting.]
Examiner and Instructor Chen comments: [It captures the intent behind promoting Wu's status.]

 toward people from afar who join in amity, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) specially promotes them for admiring righteousness. Here, Wu admired righteousness and submitted to commands at Qi, making them different from mere barbarians; even if one wished not to promote them, how could that be possible? Previously, at the meeting at Qi, Wu was referred to as "a man" (ren). There was no disparagement on our part, yet how could they be deemed worthy of meeting with? Why was this? Ever since the campaign against Tan, while the feudal lords bowed their heads in the north, the people of Wu had looked on ambitiously from the east for over ten years. Moreover, Duke Dao of Jin was a worthy hegemon, and establishing relations with Wu in order to check Chu was a righteous undertaking. Although Wu was a barbarian state that had usurped a royal title, its admiration for our Chinese customs was exceedingly firm, and its desire to participate in interstate meetings was exceedingly earnest. Therefore, regretting its failure to arrive at the upper Huai River and sending Shou Yue to seek diplomatic contact, Wu declared: "Our ruler wishes to seek blessings from Tang Shu and the two Wen [Duke Wen of Jin and King Wen of Zhou], presenting gifts of introduction and silk to have an audience with your lordship. Only because we failed to guard against the unforeseen did we miss the appointed time; our ruler dares to acknowledge his guilt." Moved by the appointment made at Shandao, and troubling Lu and Wei to announce their sincere reverence…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
也則又曰君幸惠徼于泰伯仲雍哀寡君而賜
之會寡君願與二三兄弟相見以謀其不庭君
無所辱命戚之會蓋以與中國之壇坫是幸者
而敢為主哉維時雞澤之盟內則諸侯聽命君
子以吳之來也其心同于友邦矣嘉父之款外
則諸戎事晉君子以吳之來也其事異乎夷狄
矣此之不進而亦從于柤之例待之是使夷不
變夏而中國不伸於夷也故特稱人以進之蓋
聖人之情春秋之義如此云於乎晉之通吳猶
===
楚之通秦也楚抑吳興儒者或謂悼非策然以
吳當秦悼亦籌之審矣惟晉無悼而後吳興故
夫儒者之論是責人於無已也
禮記
大德不官大道不器
蔡德璋
同考試官訓導楊批講不官不器有分别而
華藻蔚然
考試官教諭胡批典雅不浮
punctuated:
也，則又曰：「君幸惠徼于泰伯、仲雍，哀寡君而賜之會。寡君願與二三兄弟相見，以謀其不庭，君無所辱命。」戚之會，蓋以與中國之壇坫是幸者，而敢為主哉？維時雞澤之盟，內則諸侯聽命，君子以吳之來也，其心同于友邦矣；嘉父之款，外則諸戎事晉，君子以吳之來也，其事異乎夷狄矣。此之不進，而亦從于柤之例待之，是使夷不變夏，而中國不伸於夷也，故特稱「人」以進之。蓋聖人之情、《春秋》之義如此云。於乎！晉之通吳，猶楚之通秦也。楚抑吳興，儒者或謂悼非策；然以吳當秦，悼亦籌之審矣。惟晉無悼而後吳興，故夫儒者之論，是責人於無已也。

《禮記》
「大德不官，大道不器。」
蔡德璋
同考試官訓導楊批：講「不官」、「不器」有分别，而華藻蔚然。
考試官教諭胡批：典雅不浮。
translation_en:
… he further said: "Your Lordship has graciously sought blessing from the spirits of Taibo and Zhongyong, taking pity on our ruler and granting him this meeting. Our ruler wishes to meet with a few brother states to take counsel against those who do not come to court, so that Your Lordship's commands may suffer no disgrace." At the meeting at Qi, Wu considered itself fortunate merely to participate at the altar of interstate meetings of the Central States—how would it dare to act as the host? At that time, through the covenant at Jize, within the realm the feudal lords obeyed Jin's commands; thus the gentleman judged that in Wu's coming, its heart was the same as that of the friendly states. Through the overtures of Jiafu, outside the realm the various Rong tribes served Jin; thus the gentleman judged that in Wu's coming, its conduct differed from that of the Yi and Di barbarians. If one did not advance Wu in status here, and instead treated it according to the precedent of the meeting at Cha, that would prevent barbarians from transforming according to Chinese ways and keep the Central States from extending their authority over the barbarians. Therefore the text specially refers to Wu as "men" (ren) in order to advance them. Such indeed were the sentiments of the Sage and the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). Alas! Jin's establishing relations with Wu was just like Chu's establishing relations with Qin. Because Chu was checked and Wu rose to power, some Confucian scholars say that Duke Dao pursued a mistaken policy. Yet in using Wu to counter Qin, Duke Dao had calculated the matter thoroughly. It was only after Jin no longer had a ruler like Duke Dao that Wu rose to dominance; therefore, the criticism of those scholars is a case of demanding perfection of others without end.

Record of Rites (Liji)
"Great virtue does not confine itself to a single office; the great Way does not confine itself to a single vessel."
Cai Dezhang 蔡德璋
Comment by Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Yang: The explanation of "not confining to an office" and "not confining to a vessel" makes clear distinctions, and its literary elegance is lush and flourishing.
Comment by Examiner, Instructor Hu: Classically elegant and free of superficiality.

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
考試官敎諭陳批俊逸
惟道德之大者其用不能限焉蓋凡用之可限
者必本之未盛也曾謂道德之大而限於用哉
嘗謂君子之學以蘊于心而非無用也以效于
用而非無體也觀于聖道而知體用之相須矣
彼德之小者度德而官之誰曰不可惟天下有
大德彼其涵養甚充而其所蘊藉甚深也吾知
理煩治劇何所用而不宜任大投艱何所效而
不稱其始若未嘗以一長名而天下有太責任
===
於斯人乎負荷之而其蘊卒不可窺也若曰德
之各一其任如官之不相攝豈所以論於大德
者哉道之小者隨材而器之誰曰不可惟天下
有大道彼其抱負甚宏而其所設施者甚裕也
紛然臨之而泛應有全能卒然投之而妙用無
應迹其始若未嘗以一藝見而天下有大事功
於斯人乎運量之而其用卒不可究也若曰道
之各一其用如器之不相通豈所以論于大道
者哉吁惟不官然後見聖人之德惟不器然後
punctuated:
考試官敎諭陳批：俊逸。

惟道德之大者，其用不能限焉。蓋凡用之可限者，必本之未盛也。曾謂道德之大，而限於用哉？嘗謂君子之學，以蘊于心而非無用也，以效于用而非無體也。觀于聖道，而知體用之相須矣。彼德之小者，度德而官之，誰曰不可？惟天下有大德，彼其涵養甚充，而其所蘊藉甚深也。吾知理煩治劇，何所用而不宜？任大投艱，何所效而不稱？其始若未嘗以一長名，而天下有太責任，於斯人乎負荷之，而其蘊卒不可窺也。若曰德之各一其任，如官之不相攝，豈所以論於大德者哉？道之小者，隨材而器之，誰曰不可？惟天下有大道，彼其抱負甚宏，而其所設施者甚裕也。紛然臨之，而泛應有全能；卒然投之，而妙用無應迹。其始若未嘗以一藝見，而天下有大事功，於斯人乎運量之，而其用卒不可究也。若曰道之各一其用，如器之不相通，豈所以論于大道者哉？吁！惟不官，然後見聖人之德；惟不器，然後
translation_en:
Examiner and Instructor Chen comments: Outstanding and spirited.

Only when virtue and the Way are great can their function not be limited. Indeed, whenever function can be limited, it must be that the foundation is not yet abundant. Could it ever be said that when virtue and the Way are great, they are limited in their function? It has been said that in the learning of the gentleman, as it is stored in the mind, it is not without function; as it is applied in function, it is not without substance. By observing the Way of the sage, one knows that substance and function depend upon each other. As for those of lesser virtue, if one measures their virtue and assigns them a specific office, who would say that is unacceptable? Only in the world is there great virtue: his self-cultivation is exceedingly full, and what he stores up within is exceedingly deep. I know that in managing complexities and governing burdensome affairs, where could he be used and not be suitable? In taking on great responsibilities and being cast into difficulties, what effect could he render that would not match the task? In the beginning, he seems never to have been known for a single specialty, yet when the world has great responsibilities, they are borne upon this person's shoulders, and what he stores within can ultimately never be fathomed. If one were to say that virtue is each confined to a single responsibility, just as offices do not overlap in jurisdiction, how could this be a way to discuss great virtue? As for the lesser ways, if one follows a person's talent and treats him as a specialized implement, who would say that is unacceptable? Only in the world is there the great Way: his aspirations are exceedingly vast, and what he puts into practice is exceedingly ample. When affairs press upon him in confusion, he responds broadly with complete capability; when tasks are suddenly cast upon him, his marvelous function leaves no trace of its response. In the beginning, he seems never to have distinguished himself by a single skill, yet when the world has great achievements to be accomplished, they are managed and measured by this person, and his function can ultimately never be exhausted. If one were to say that the Way is each confined to a single function, just as implements are not interchangeable, how could this be a way to discuss the great Way? Ah! Only by not being confined to a single office is the virtue of the sage then seen; only by not being a specialized implement is…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
見聖人之道君子察此可有志於本矣斯人也
惟夫子足以當之觀其學殫累世藝兼多能其
却萊兵反侵地墮名都視天下事皆緒使也若
以偏材而欲輒試于用則窒而不達卽欲以狡
獪猥調託之于通方而曰我且不官我且不器
謬矣學者可不務本哉
爲人君者謹其所好惡而已矣君好之則
臣爲之上行之則民從之詩云誘民孔
易此之謂也
===
翟廷策
同考試官訓導楊批根極理趣一洗塵言是
大雅文字
考試官敎諭胡批說謹字見理
考試官敎諭陳批明暢
論君心之當愼以其感人之易也蓋好惡通於
臣民皆之誘人易矣徵於詩而可不愼與且夫
人君託於音樂以明其敎非徒自娛於音也將
以通天下之感也是故德音溺音邪正辨矣而
punctuated:
見聖人之道。君子察此，可有志於本矣。斯人也，惟夫子足以當之。觀其學殫累世，藝兼多能，其却萊兵、反侵地、墮名都，視天下事皆緒使也。若以偏材而欲輒試于用，則窒而不達；卽欲以狡獪猥調託之于通方，而曰：「我且不官，我且不器」，謬矣！學者可不務本哉？

「爲人君者，謹其所好惡而已矣。君好之則臣爲之，上行之則民從之。《詩》云：『誘民孔易。』此之謂也。」
翟廷策
同考試官訓導楊批：根極理趣，一洗塵言，是大雅文字。
考試官敎諭胡批：說「謹」字見理。
考試官敎諭陳批：明暢。

論君心之當愼，以其感人之易也。蓋好惡通於臣民，皆之誘人易矣。徵於《詩》，而可不愼與？且夫人君託於音樂以明其敎，非徒自娛於音也，將以通天下之感也。是故德音、溺音，邪正辨矣。而
translation_en:
… manifests the Way of the sage. Examining this, the gentleman can set his ambition upon the fundamental. As for such a person, only the Master is worthy of answering to it. Observing how his learning exhausted the knowledge of successive generations and his skills encompassed manifold abilities—his repelling the troops of Lai, recovering the invaded lands, and dismantling the famous capitals—he regarded all the affairs of the world as mere secondary tasks to be dispatched. If one possesses only partial talent yet wishes to rashly test it in practical use, one will be obstructed and fail to get through. And if one wishes to pass off crafty and vulgar versatility as comprehensive mastery, saying, "I am neither bound to a single office, nor confined to a single vessel," how absurd that is! How can scholars not devote themselves to the fundamental?

"One who is a ruler of men simply takes care regarding what he likes and dislikes. What the ruler likes, the ministers will do; what the superior practices, the common people will follow. The Book of Odes (Shi) says, 'To guide the people is very easy.' This is what is meant."
Zhai Tingce 翟廷策
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Yang 楊 comments: Grounded in the ultimate meaning of principle, it washes away mundane words; this is a composition of great elegance.
Examiner and Instructor Hu 胡 comments: The explanation of the word "take care" (jin 謹) shows grasp of principle.
Examiner and Instructor Chen 陳 comments: Clear and fluent.

This discusses why the ruler's mind must be cautious, because it moves others so easily. Indeed, likes and dislikes communicate themselves to ministers and the people; in both cases [?], guiding others is easy. Verified against the Book of Odes, how could one not be cautious? Moreover, a ruler of men entrusts his sentiments to music in order to clarify his teachings; it is not merely to amuse himself with sounds, but rather to communicate sentiments throughout the world. Therefore, between virtuous music and decadent music, the distinction between perverse and upright is clear. And for…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
爲人君者可不謹其好惡哉當知以好感者其
心易以淫君無以其淫者爲好也以謹其好必
要諸德音即弗入於心必察矣以惡感者其心
易以私君無以其私者爲惡也以謹其惡必要
諸溺音即習移於心弗顧矣所以當謹者曷故
哉正以臣不自爲惟君是爲君誠好矣臣即相
率而爲焉不問其所好何如也民無定從惟上
是從上誠行矣民即相率而從焉不問其所行
何如也此其爲之本在君不在臣從之機在上
===
不在下誘民何易易耶觀詩以誘民語君德以
孔易道民心正此好即爲行即從之謂也然則
謹其好惡孰非謹其誘民者哉而子夏之言進
乎音矣嗟乎人主之好惡易溺豈直是哉端儒
莊士程容於柔曼則遠親巽亢言激論角聽於
頌媚則距內異始之中其所好者不一二人既
則諧臣肩比諛歌耳滿爲而從之成風矣人主
達於子夏之說者何論聲音即通於政治可也
第貳場
punctuated:
爲人君者，可不謹其好惡哉？當知以好感者，其心易以淫，君無以其淫者爲好也；以謹其好，必要諸德音，即弗入於心，必察矣。以惡感者，其心易以私，君無以其私者爲惡也；以謹其惡，必要諸溺音，即習移於心，弗顧矣。所以當謹者曷故哉？正以臣不自爲，惟君是爲，君誠好矣，臣即相率而爲焉，不問其所好何如也。民無定從，惟上是從，上誠行矣，民即相率而從焉，不問其所行何如也。此其爲之本在君不在臣，從之機在上不在下，誘民何易易耶！觀《詩》以「誘民」語君德，以「孔易」道民心，正此好即爲、行即從之謂也。然則謹其好惡，孰非謹其誘民者哉？而子夏之言進乎音矣。嗟乎！人主之好惡易溺，豈直是哉？端儒莊士，程容於柔曼，則遠親巽；亢言激論，角聽於頌媚，則距內異。始之中其所好者不一二人，既則諧臣肩比、諛歌耳滿，爲而從之，成風矣。人主達於子夏之說者，何論聲音？即通於政治可也。
第貳場
translation_en:
…how could one who acts as a ruler not be cautious with his likes and dislikes? He ought to know that when moved by fondness, the mind easily falls into dissipation; thus the ruler must not take what is dissipative as his fondness. To be cautious in his likes, he must verify them against virtuous sounds; even if they do not immediately appeal to his mind, he must examine them closely. When moved by aversion, the mind easily falls into partiality; thus the ruler must not take his personal biases as his aversion. To be cautious in his dislikes, he must verify them against decadent sounds; even if habit has shifted his mind toward them, he must pay them no heed.

Why is it that he must be so cautious? Precisely because ministers do not act of their own accord, but act only according to the ruler: if the ruler truly likes something, his ministers will lead one another to practice it, without asking what his fondness is like. The common people have no fixed allegiance, but follow only their superiors: if superiors truly carry something out, the people will lead one another to follow it, without asking what their conduct is like. Thus, the root of action lies with the ruler and not the ministers, and the pivot of compliance lies with superiors and not inferiors—how very easy it is to guide the people! When we observe that the Book of Odes (Shi) speaks of the ruler's virtue in terms of "guiding the people," and describes the people's minds as "exceedingly easy," it refers precisely to this principle: that what is liked is immediately practiced, and what is carried out is immediately followed. If this is so, then in being cautious about his likes and dislikes, is he not being cautious about how he guides the people? Thus the words of Zixia 子夏 advance beyond mere music.

Alas! That a sovereign's likes and dislikes easily sink into indulgence—is it merely in this matter of music? When upright Confucians and dignified gentlemen have their demeanor measured against the soft and alluring, the ruler distances the親 [?] and favors the compliant; when forthright words and vigorous counsels compete for a hearing against eulogies and flattery, he rejects them and harbors the divergent [?]. At first, those who cater to his likes are no more than one or two men; before long, sycophantic ministers stand shoulder to shoulder, and flattering songs fill his ears, until practicing and following them becomes the prevailing custom. For a sovereign who grasps the meaning of Zixia's discourse, why speak only of sounds and music? It can be applied directly to governance as well.

Second Session

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
論
王者如天
梁維屏
同考試官教諭姚批格調古雅含蓄泓深說
如天本旨最親切有味非邃養不能
同考試官教諭高批不事馳騁而淵然蒼然
純是大家機軸敬服敬服
考試官教諭胡批論王道甚精透誦之悠
然
===
考試官教諭陳批就題立說先進之文
聖人以無心治天下故天下忘乎聖人之治天
下忘乎聖人之治而聖人之治益大彼天下羣
生喁喁然待命於聖人而聖人者以一人制天
下之命有羣衆則有是非有是非則有刑賞有
刑賞則有喜怒聖人豈異人哉奈何以無心治
之而能使天下與之相忘也嗟乎此聖人之治
所以爲大洪濛寥廓覆之如天舉萬物終始於
其中而不自知也今夫天太虛無垠譬之橐籥
punctuated:
論
王者如天
梁維屏
同考試官教諭姚批：格調古雅，含蓄泓深，說「如天」本旨最親切有味，非邃養不能。
同考試官教諭高批：不事馳騁，而淵然蒼然，純是大家機軸，敬服敬服。
考試官教諭胡批：論王道甚精透，誦之悠然。
考試官教諭陳批：就題立說，先進之文。
聖人以無心治天下，故天下忘乎聖人之治；天下忘乎聖人之治，而聖人之治益大。彼天下羣生，喁喁然待命於聖人，而聖人者以一人制天下之命。有羣衆則有是非，有是非則有刑賞，有刑賞則有喜怒，聖人豈異人哉？奈何以無心治之，而能使天下與之相忘也？嗟乎！此聖人之治所以爲大。洪濛寥廓，覆之如天，舉萬物終始於其中而不自知也。今夫天，太虛無垠，譬之橐籥，
translation_en:
Discourse (lun)

"A True King is Like Heaven"

Liang Weiping 梁維屏

Comment by Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Yao 姚: The style is antique and elegant, reserved and deeply profound. In explaining the fundamental purport of "like Heaven," it is most intimate and full of flavor—something impossible without deep cultivation.

Comment by Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Gao 高: Without indulging in unbridled display, it is deep and venerable in tone, purely the loom and axle of a great master. Truly admirable, truly admirable!

Comment by Examiner and County Director of Studies Hu 胡: Its discussion of the Kingly Way is exceedingly penetrating; reciting it leaves one in lingering contemplation.

Comment by Examiner and County Director of Studies Chen 陳: It constructs its argument directly from the theme—prose in the style of the worthies of former generations.

The sage governs the world with an uncalculating mind; therefore, the world forgets the sage's governance. When the world forgets the sage's governance, the sage's governance becomes all the greater. Those myriad living beings of the world look up expectantly, awaiting their ordination from the sage, while the sage, as a single man, regulates the destiny of the world. Where there are multitudes, there are right and wrong; where there are right and wrong, there are punishments and rewards; where there are punishments and rewards, there are joy and anger. How is the sage any different from other men? How then can he govern it with an uncalculating mind and cause the world to forget him? Alas! This is why the governance of the sage is great. Vast, primordial, and boundless, he covers all things like Heaven, so that the myriad things complete their endings and beginnings within it without realizing it themselves. Now consider Heaven: the Great Void is boundless, and if we liken it to a bellows…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
鼓以二氣運以四時吸之噓之通之復之吸則
寒噓則暑通則元亨復則利貞一翕一闢互爲
其根其榮茂也物不以爲德其凋落也物不以
爲怨何則無心故也天無心以萬物爲心榮茂
凋落皆物所自取故曰栽者培之傾者覆之因
材而篤而天無與焉人則各一其心形骸格于
外情識橫乎中同我者是異我者非是我而予
之者德非我而奪之者怨棼棼藉藉莫適爲主
有聖人者出是天建于天下而全畀以所覆乃
===
相率而聽命於聖人故聖人繼天而王者有覆
冒天下者也洪範有之惟辟作威惟辟作福王
者操威福之柄可以養人可以教人可以榮人
辱人可以生人殺人而以有心與之舉天下惟
吾所欲爲而莫之敢抗將恣意肆行何所不至
而天下之后我者讎我者各任其喜怒交起而
爭王者亦人耳何以覆冒天下蓋嘗讀史至陶
唐之世而神游其天彼其出而作入而息鑿飲
而耕食孰非受放勳之賜者乃擊壤而歌帝力
punctuated: 鼓以二氣，運以四時，吸之噓之，通之復之。吸則寒，噓則暑；通則元亨，復則利貞。一翕一闢，互爲其根。其榮茂也，物不以爲德；其凋落也，物不以爲怨。何則？無心故也。天無心，以萬物爲心，榮茂凋落，皆物所自取。故曰：「栽者培之，傾者覆之。」因材而篤，而天無與焉。人則各一其心，形骸格于外，情識橫乎中。同我者是，異我者非；是我而予之者德，非我而奪之者怨。棼棼藉藉，莫適爲主。有聖人者出，是天建于天下，而全畀以所覆，乃相率而聽命於聖人。故聖人繼天而王者，有覆冒天下者也。《洪範》有之：「惟辟作威，惟辟作福。」王者操威福之柄，可以養人，可以教人，可以榮人辱人，可以生人殺人。而以有心與之，舉天下惟吾所欲爲而莫之敢抗，將恣意肆行，何所不至？而天下之后我者、讎我者，各任其喜怒，交起而爭。王者亦人耳，何以覆冒天下？蓋嘗讀史至陶唐之世，而神游其天。彼其出而作，入而息，鑿飲而耕食，孰非受放勳之賜者？乃擊壤而歌：「帝力…
translation_en:
…stirred by the two vital forces (yin and yang) and revolved through the four seasons, inhaling and exhaling, expanding and returning. Its inhalation brings cold, and its exhalation brings heat; its expansion brings origination and flourishing (yuanheng), and its return brings advantage and firmness (lizhen). Closing and opening, each serves as the root of the other. When things flourish and thrive, they do not regard it as a favor; when they wither and fall, they do not regard it with resentment. Why is this? Because Heaven has no deliberate mind of its own. Heaven has no mind of its own, taking the myriad things as its mind; flourishing and withering are both brought upon themselves by things. Thus it is said: "What is planted it nourishes; what is tilting it overthrows." It strengthens things according to their own qualities, and Heaven has no personal involvement therein.

Men, however, each have their own individual mind; physical forms separate them on the outside, while passions and perceptions run rampant within. Those who agree with me are deemed right, and those who differ from me are deemed wrong; those who affirm me and give to me are met with gratitude, while those who fault me and take from me are met with resentment. In tangled confusion and clamorous disorder, there is no one whom they can agree to follow as master. When a sage appears, he is established by Heaven over the world and entrusted completely with all that Heaven covers, so people lead one another to obey the commands of the sage. Therefore, the sage who succeeds Heaven as a true king is one who covers and shelters the entire world.

The Great Plan (Hongfan) has it: "Only the sovereign makes awe-inspiring punishment; only the sovereign makes blessing." The true king holds the handle of punishment and blessing: he can nourish men, teach men, honor or disgrace men, and give life to or put to death men. Yet if he deals with them with a deliberate, self-interested mind—supposing that across the whole world he alone may do whatever he desires and none dare resist him—he will indulge his whims and act without restraint, stopping at nothing. Then those in the world who treat me as sovereign and those who treat me as an enemy will each give rein to their own joy and anger, rising up together in contention. The true king is also merely a man; how then could he cover and shelter the world?

Indeed, I have read history down to the age of Tao Tang (Emperor Yao) and let my spirit roam in his Heaven-like realm. Those people went out to work at sunrise and came in to rest at sunset, dug wells to drink and plowed fields to eat—who among them was not receiving the bounty of Fangxun (Yao)? Yet they beat the ground and sang: "What is the Emperor's power…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
何有於我哉立我烝民莫非爾極矣而康衢之
謠方且不識不知吾以是知天之爲大而堯之
爲天也故曰大哉堯之爲君巍巍乎則天蕩蕩
乎無能名夫王者不以我治天下而以天下治
天下以我治天下者民寒而曰我衣之也民饑
而曰我食之也民遠於善而曰我敎之也民陷
於罪而曰我刑之也上知有我下亦知有我上
有我故任威福下有我故任德怨威福德怨交
于上下而喜怒叢生淳化日漓善乎禹之言曰
===
堯舜之民皆以堯舜之心爲心至於予而百姓
各自以其心爲心蓋慮之矣欲通天下以爲心
則莫若以天之心爲心以天之心爲心故知有
天下不知有我不知有我故有心於天下治無
心於治天下以無心治天下故上不任威福下
亦不任德怨皇極之敷言有之無偏無陂遵王
之義無有作好遵王之道無有作惡遵王之路
故未甞衣食天下而農人舉趾紅女在機民以
爲自給自足而王者不言澤未甞提命天下而
punctuated: 何有於我哉！」立我烝民，莫非爾極矣，而康衢之謠方且「不識不知」。吾以是知天之爲大，而堯之爲天也。故曰：「大哉堯之爲君，巍巍乎則天，蕩蕩乎無能名。」夫王者不以我治天下，而以天下治天下。以我治天下者，民寒而曰：「我衣之也。」民饑而曰：「我食之也。」民遠於善而曰：「我敎之也。」民陷於罪而曰：「我刑之也。」上知有我，下亦知有我。上有我，故任威福；下有我，故任德怨。威福、德怨交于上下，而喜怒叢生，淳化日漓。善乎禹之言曰：「堯、舜之民，皆以堯、舜之心爲心；至於予，而百姓各自以其心爲心。」蓋慮之矣。欲通天下以爲心，則莫若以天之心爲心。以天之心爲心，故知有天下，不知有我；不知有我，故有心於天下治，無心於治天下。以無心治天下，故上不任威福，下亦不任德怨。皇極之敷言有之：「無偏無陂，遵王之義；無有作好，遵王之道；無有作惡，遵王之路。」故未甞衣食天下，而農人舉趾、紅女在機，民以爲自給自足，而王者不言澤；未甞提命天下，而
translation_en:
… has the Emperor's power to do with me?" In establishing our multitudes of people, everything came from his supreme standard; yet the ballad of the highroad spoke of "not knowing and not being conscious." By this I know that Heaven is great, and that Yao was like Heaven. Therefore it is said: "Great indeed was Yao as a sovereign! How lofty, in that he modeled himself on Heaven; how vast, so that the people could find no name for it!"

Now, a true king does not govern the world through his own ego, but governs the world through the world itself. One who governs the world through his own ego says, when the people are cold, "I clothe them"; when the people are hungry, he says, "I feed them"; when the people are far from goodness, he says, "I instruct them"; when the people fall into crime, he says, "I punish them." When the ruler above is conscious of his ego, those below are also conscious of their egos. Because the ruler above has an ego, he relies on his power toawe and to reward; because those below have egos, they give way to gratitude and resentment. When awe and reward, gratitude and resentment intersect between above and below, joy and anger spring up in profusion, and pure transformation daily grows thin. Admirable indeed are the words of Yu: "The people of Yao and Shun all took the mind of Yao and Shun as their own mind; by the time it came to me, the hundred surnames each took their own minds as their minds." Indeed, he was concerned about this!

If one wishes to unite the whole world into a single mind, nothing is better than taking the mind of Heaven as one's mind. By taking the mind of Heaven as one's mind, one is conscious of the world and not conscious of one's ego; not being conscious of one's ego, one has a mind for the world's being well-governed, yet has no deliberate mind to govern the world. Governing the world without deliberate mind, the ruler above does not rely on awe and reward, nor do those below give way to gratitude and resentment. The ampliamente set forth words of the Supreme Standard have it: "Without deflection, without unevenness, pursue the royal righteousness; without selfish likings, pursue the royal way; without selfish dislikings, pursue the royal path." Therefore, he never deliberately clothed or fed the world, yet farmers lifted their feet to plow and weaving women were at their looms; the people considered themselves self-supplied and self-sufficient, and the true king did not speak of his bounty. He never personally enjoined and instructed the world, yet…

title: 萬曆十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
司徒敬敷典樂克諧民以爲自親自遜而王者
不言化未嘗敲扑天下而五聲兼聽三居克允
民以爲自恥自格而王者不言威我惠民而視
以爲雨露之滋我明民而視以爲曜曦之照我
戮民而視以爲風霆之震霜雪之肅當其時協
氣横流懷生浡潏固無咨嗟怨嘆之聲亦無感
恩圖報之迹上之心常通於下不出廟堂而九
垓八埏之外若端委而化下之心常通於上無
事煦沫而踵武逖聽之夫若玄默而信故曰王
===
者如天不令人喜不令人怒也彼偏霸之徒爲
驩虞之治欲以力征經營天下筭計見效似捷
於王者而不知其囿於天覆之中直醯雞視之
耳會葵丘示義安知大義問包茅示禮安知大
禮伐原示信安知大信戰泓示仁安知大仁故
曰眇乎小哉所以屬於人警乎大哉獨成其天
此天人之辨也夫天之所生孰非肖天者而自
棄於天則有我之心累之故同天者忘己希天
者克己不令人喜不令人怒王道之大也無有
punctuated: 司徒敬敷，典樂克諧，民以爲自親自遜，而王者不言化；未嘗敲扑天下，而五聲兼聽，三居克允，民以爲自恥自格，而王者不言威。我惠民，而視以爲雨露之滋；我明民，而視以爲曜曦之照；我戮民，而視以爲風霆之震、霜雪之肅。當其時，協氣横流，懷生浡潏，固無咨嗟怨嘆之聲，亦無感恩圖報之迹。上之心常通於下，不出廟堂，而九垓八埏之外，若端委而化；下之心常通於上，無事煦沫，而踵武逖聽之夫，若玄默而信。故曰：「王者如天，不令人喜，不令人怒也。」彼偏霸之徒，爲驩虞之治，欲以力征經營天下，筭計見效，似捷於王者，而不知其囿於天覆之中，直醯雞視之耳。會葵丘示義，安知大義？問包茅示禮，安知大禮？伐原示信，安知大信？戰泓示仁，安知大仁？故曰：「眇乎小哉，所以屬於人；警乎大哉，獨成其天。」此天人之辨也。夫天之所生，孰非肖天者？而自棄於天，則有我之心累之。故同天者忘己，希天者克己。不令人喜，不令人怒，王道之大也；無有
translation_en:
… the Minister of Education respectfully spreads the teachings and the Director of Music achieves harmony, the people regard their affection and deference as arising from themselves, and the true king does not speak of his transforming influence. Though he has never flogged the world into submission, yet by listening simultaneously to the five sounds of litigation and justly apportioning the three locales of banishment, the people feel shame and reform of their own accord, and the true king does not speak of his majesty. When I bestow favor on the people, they view it as the nourishing moisture of rain and dew; when I enlighten the people, they view it as the illumination of the bright sun; when I punish the people, they view it as the shock of wind and thunder or the severity of frost and snow. At such a time, harmonious ether flows everywhere and living beings teem with vitality; there are decidedly no sounds of sighing or bitter complaint, nor any traces of feeling obliged to repay favors. The mind of the ruler is constantly in communion with those below: without stepping outside the ancestral temple and court, beyond the nine regions and eight borders it is as if he sits in ceremonial robes and transforms them. The minds of those below are constantly in communion with the ruler: without need for petty acts of mutual moistening, those who follow in his footsteps and listen from afar trust him as if in profound silence. Therefore it is said: "The true king is like Heaven; he neither makes men rejoice nor makes men angry."

As for those partial hegemons, they practice a governance of superficial merriment, wishing to manage the world through forceful conquest. In calculating immediate results, they seem faster than the true king, yet they do not realize that they remain confined within the canopy of Heaven, to be viewed merely like vinegar-flies in a jar. Assembling at Kuiqiu to display righteousness—what did that have to do with great righteousness? Inquiring about the bundled tribute-reeds to display ritual propriety—what did that have to do with great ritual propriety? Attacking Yuan to display trustworthiness—what did that have to do with great trustworthiness? Fighting at the Hong River to display benevolence—what did that have to do with great benevolence? Therefore it is said: "Petty and small indeed is that by which one belongs to the merely human; awe-inspiring and great indeed is he who alone perfects his Heaven-nature!" This is the distinction between Heaven and man.

Now, among all whom Heaven gives birth to, who does not resemble Heaven? That one abandons oneself from Heaven is because a self-centered mind encumbers one. Therefore, he who is one with Heaven forgets himself, and he who aspires to Heaven overcomes himself. Neither making men rejoice nor making men angry—such is the greatness of the Kingly Way. Having no…

國之意當是作手

translation_en:
… indulging in personal likes and indulging in personal dislikes—that is the purity of the kingly mind. Those who aspire to the Kingly Way need only begin with their minds.

Huang Rugui 黄如桂

Associate Examiner and Instructor Gao's comment: Broadly learned without being exhausted in diction, ornate without suffering from over-artfulness; this is someone adept at crafting parallel couplets.
Examiner and Instructor Hu's comment: Allusive, rich, and well-regulated.
Examiner and Instructor Chen's comment: Rich in learning and skillful in phrasing; worthy of selection.
